zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Review sources: Native scan, Bibliothèque nationale de France / Gallica. Secondary lexical check: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, developed by Hideyuki Ohshima with assistance from Taichi Aida, licensed CC BY 4.0 (official release: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). The transcription corrections and English notes are original scan-grounded review work; the lexical data and generated reading hints do not determine diplomatic spelling.

lines.note: Saimon is explained by futatabi too, asking a second time. This is the repeated-question sense, distinct from the western gate in the next entry; the printed circumflex in tô is retained.
Vez completes 'a segunda vez', a second time. The final S labels written usage rather than supplying another part of the Japanese expression. The standalone S. is upright, outside the italic gloss.
This Saimon is nishi no mon, a gate on the western side. The Portuguese directional phrase continues into Poente on the following row.
Poente, the west or sunset side, completes the gate definition. The short continuation is a separate physical line, not a new entry.

Sainami denotes afflicting or tormenting someone. The principal parts and the caron in ǒda are retained rather than regularized to modern verb forms; the Portuguese affliction verb has a compressed impression. Enlargement confirms the anomalous Affigir without an l; it is not silently expanded to Affligir.
Sainan is explained as komaka and yawaraka, fine and soft. This material-quality sense is distinguished from the following homonymous word for misfortune.

runs.text: brãda, & delgada, como peça de ſeda.

lines.note: The Portuguese continues with softness and thinness, using a piece of silk as the example. Brãda retains its printed abbreviation, and S marks written usage. The final S. is an upright register label.
This Sainan is wazawai or nangi, calamity and hardship. Perigos and the divided ma- begin a list of dangers, evils, and troubles completed below.
Les completes ma-les, and trabalhos adds troubles or hardships. The whole list explains the adverse-event sense of Sainan.
Sai no kawara is described through the mission's comparison with the limbo of children. This is the dictionary's explanatory analogy, not an assertion that the two religious concepts are identical.

runs.text: na outra vida, ſegundo a opinião dos gentios.

lines.note: The place is situated in the next life and attributed to the beliefs of the people called gentios in the source. The Portuguese qualification belongs to the preceding religious description.
Saikyo is glossed by kuji wo tadasu, investigating a legal dispute. The scan's descending j supports Cujiuo rather than OCR Cuiiuo; de- starts demanda below.
Demanda completes the legal-case gloss. Kuji no saikyo is then illustrated as questions or inquiries concerning the dispute; the following line completes the explanation.
Exame sobre a demanda completes the example as examination of the lawsuit. This continuation is not another Japanese headword.

Saiqin is explained by moyoo(sh)i tsutomuru, urging or undertaking an action. The Portuguese O por por begins the construction 'put into practice'; the repeated por is not an accidental duplicated word to delete.
Obra completes por por obra, putting something into effect, followed by executar. The written-register label S closes the entry. The terminal S. is set upright.
Saikwai is meeting again, paraphrased as futatabi oo. The initial v in vǒ belongs to the historical spelling; the Portuguese begins meeting or seeing one another again.

runs.text: ſe, & falarſe duas vezes, ou a ſegunda vez.

lines.note: The continuation completes ver-se and adds speaking together twice or for the second time. It explains the reciprocal reunion sense of Saiquai.
Saiquat is coming back to life, explained by futatabi yomigayeru. The final t is the printed checked ending and is not expanded; the Portuguese resurrection verb is divided across rows.
Tar completes Reſuſci-tar. Saiquat suru supplies the verbal construction for being restored to life, followed by the written-register label S. The S. label after the Japanese example is upright.
Sairai is a second coming, literally futatabi kitaru. The Portuguese specifies whose return is meant on the next line; dal- is a genuine line-end division.
Gum completes dal-gum: the return is of a Cami or Fotoque. Both Japanese religious terms occur inside the Portuguese explanation rather than as independent headwords.
Sairei denotes a ritual festival, with matsurigoto and rei as the Japanese explanation. The Portuguese begins describing celebrations held for a deity.
Fazem ao Cami completes the festival definition, specifying its recipient. Cami is a Japanese religious term embedded in the Portuguese sentence.
Saireoo denotes an escort or guard for goods, explained by nimot no keigo. Nimotno retains the printed checked-t form rather than being expanded to a modern nimotsu spelling; vi- begins vigia below.

runs.text: gia que vai com o fato.

lines.note: Gia completes vigia, the person who accompanies the goods. Fato here refers to baggage or possessions, not the modern abstract meaning 'fact'.

Sairon is discussing or debating a matter again, as futatabi ronzuru explains. Reinspection of the rounded but abraded vowel supports ron rather than the OCR's ren; the Portuguese likewise specifies repetition.
Vezes a cousa completes discussing the matter twice. This is the continuation of Sairon, not a separate frequency headword.
Saisai means many times or repeatedly, exactly the sense of Muitas vezes. The internal long ſ is retained.
Saisan is explained by futatabi and mitabi, twice and three times. The Portuguese number phrase continues with vezes on the next line.
Saisan mooshita means having said something repeatedly. The Portuguese begins 'I have already spoken two-', with du- completed on the following physical row.

runs.text: as, ou tres vezes, ou muitas vezes.

lines.note: As completes du-as, followed by 'or three times, or many times'. The OCR's internal space in vezes is removed after checking the damaged but continuous word.

runs.text: Eruas que ſe comem, ou or-

lines.note: Saisoo is equated with yasai and glossed as edible greens. Enlargement shows a round s, not OCR g, before the caroned vowel; the damaged a is retained from the surviving word. The spelling is not normalized to the next entry's Saiſo.
Taliça completes or-taliça, vegetables or garden greens. This brief continuation closes the preceding edible-plants entry.
Saiso contrasts komashi and arashi, fine and coarse. The Portuguese likewise juxtaposes miuda and grossa; these are contrasting qualities, not a malformed single adjective.
Sa completes groſ-ſa. Vide directs the reader to Sosai, the reversed compound, and the Japanese cross-reference remains distinct from the italic Portuguese instruction.
Saisoku denotes urging or persuasion, explained by moyoo(sh)i, su. The Portuguese also gives counsel, with cõ- continued below; the nasal abbreviation is preserved.

runs.text: ſelho. Item, Aliquando, perſuaſão forte a-

lines.note: Selho completes cõ-selho. The entry adds that the word can sometimes mean strong persuasion, with a- continuing into apertando on the next row.
The intensified sense involves pressing or constraining someone. The weak abbreviation mark over the final e supports alguẽ, retained as a chosen but faint reading; Sai- starts the example below.
Saisoku wo tsukuru introduces the practice of putting people into someone's house to enforce payment. The gloss begins the description here and continues with its purpose on the next row.

runs.text: guem pera o fazer pagar a diuida, &c.

lines.note: The people are lodged there to make the debtor pay the debt. This completes the enforcement example, not a general definition of household residence.
Saisokunin names people who urge or constrain others. The final nin, the person-denoting element, is supported by the scan; OCR Saiſocuirin is not retained.
Gem completes conſtrã-gem, and the object is some action or matter. The line finishes the definition of the people who apply pressure.
Saisui is explained as komaka ni kudaku, breaking something down finely, here applied to detailed explanation. The tightly set Muitomiuda is retained as printed rather than silently respaced.
Encarecidamente adds the sense of emphatic or earnest explanation. Saisui mooshi kika- begins the Japanese example and continues into kikase on the next row.

Xe completes kikase, followed by the polite sooro form printed without a vowel mark. The Portuguese says it was explained minutely and at length; enlargement identifies Diße, not OCR Diſce, while difuſa- continues below.
Mente completes difuſa-mente, describing an expansive or detailed explanation. This last short line closes the left column and is not page furniture.
Saitai means having a wife or being married. Sai- starts an example of describing oneself or another as a married person.
Tai completes saitai; no mi de gozaru is the construction for being in the married state. The Portuguese repeats being married or having a wife, and its terminal comma is retained.
Kano boozu wa seiso(o) de wa nai, saitai- contrasts a celibate monk with a married one. The negative nai is essential to the example; the caron and circumflex are kept occurrence by occurrence.

runs.text: Aquelle Bonzo não he dos continentes,

lines.note: Gia completes the Japanese assertion. The Portuguese says that this Bonzo is not among the continent or celibate members; the description continues below.
The continuation adds regular religious observance to the contrast and concludes that he has a wife. It belongs to the same example of Saitai.
Saitan is being born again, explained by futatabi umaruru. The historical v in vmaruru is retained rather than changed to modern u.

runs.text: vez neſte mundo como imaginão os gentios.

lines.note: The explanation locates this second birth in the present world and attributes the idea to the people termed gentios. That qualification frames the following comparison with a learned religious figure.

Monju no saitan ja calls someone a rebirth of Monju. V. G. is the introductory Latin abbreviation, not Japanese G; its type follows the italic gloss. The Portuguese introduces the kind of person to whom the phrase applies.

runs.text: hum homem muito ſabio, ou letrado no qual pa-

lines.note: The phrase is applied to a very wise or learned man. Pa- begins parece, leading into the claim that the earlier sage seems to have been reborn in him.

runs.text: rece que tornou a nacer aquelle diſcipulo muito

lines.note: Rece completes pa-rece. The learned man is likened to the rebirth of that exceptionally learned disciple; printed nacer is preserved without adding the consonant of modern nascer.
Docto de Xaca completes the description of Monju as a learned disciple of Xaca. Xaca is embedded in the Portuguese explanation, not an independent entry on this row.
Saiten is explained by hashira and taruki, a column and rafter. The Portuguese architectural terms match those two structural members.
Saiten kezurazu gives the negative construction, not hewing or dressing the columns and rafters. The doubled z is retained from the historical romanization.
The continuation names the house's columns and rafters and supplies a cross-reference to Booshi. The scan supports colũnas, not OCR colũinas; the nasal abbreviation is retained.
Saitoo is equated with Nagatana and described as a knife for cutting turnips. The caron distinguishes this printed headword from the circumflex on the following homonym.
Other greens are added to the vegetables cut with the knife. This short line ends the utensil definition before the separate vessel entry.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de ſelha em que ſe mete o

lines.note: Saitô is a kind of tub or receptacle. The gloss continues with the food it contains, and the circumflex is retained rather than made identical to the preceding knife entry.

runs.text: comer cortado, ou iguarias q̃ ão de ſair a meſa.

lines.note: The vessel holds cut-up food or dishes about to be served. The scan shows cortado, not OCR corſado; the printed q̃ and ão remain unexpanded.

Saiu is fine rain, explained by komakana ame. The irregular mark above the first o in Comacana is treated as local paper or ink damage rather than the OCR caron; this remains a nonblocking caveat because the impression is impaired. The conspicuous space in Sai v is retained, and the terminal S. is an upright written-register label.
Saiwai is glossed as opportunity or a favorable occasion. This local sense, rather than an imposed modern translation as happiness, governs the following adjectival entry.

runs.text: Couſa oportuna, ou que vem apro-

lines.note: Saiwaina describes something opportune or arriving at a suitable moment. The initial capital is an abraded S, not OCR A; apro- continues on the next line.
Posito completes apro-poſito, coming appropriately or at the right time. The row closes the adjective's explanation.
Saiwoo is explained by futatabi, a second time. The scan shows u, not OCR n, and the following example repeats the same form across the line boundary.
Sai-uoo, saihen mooshita expresses having said something time and again. The Portuguese begins 'I spoke once and', continuing on the next row; the historical spelling ſaifen is retained.
Outra completes 'once and another time', followed by the looser sense 'many times'. This closes the repetition example under Saiuǒ.

Saishaku is glossed as commenting on or explaining a book. The printed Japanese paraphrase Furatabi yerabu is retained despite its awkwardness beside that meaning; the apparent r is not silently repaired to the expected futatabi spelling.

The gloss continues with explaining a book. Qiòuo ſai- begins the example continued below; the final enlarged scan shows a single descending grave over o, so Qiòuo replaces the draft circumflex without normalizing the Japanese word for a scripture.
Xacu suru completes saishaku suru. It belongs with Qiôuo on the previous row, not to an independent headword.

runs.text: Caxas que ſe offerecem, & deitão di-

lines.note: Saisen refers here to cash offered before a deity. The Portuguese Caxas is the printed money term. A short double-bar line-end hyphen is visible after di, beginning di-ante across the break; the hyphen is restored rather than dropping the edge mark.

Ante completes diante. The offerings are made before a Fotoque or Cami; the capital C and vowel a are visible. Saixenuo begins the Japanese example, with n rather than the OCR's r and without its spurious internal space.
Mairasuru completes saisen wo mairasuru, presenting the offerings. Offerecer estas caxas restates the action in Portuguese.
Saishi is explained as kami wo matsuru koto, honoring a deity ritually. The Portuguese begins 'festival or ceremony', continued below.

runs.text: ceremonia que ſe faz aos Camis.

lines.note: Ceremonia completes the ritual definition, specifying ceremonies for the Camis. The Portuguese plural ending on the borrowed religious term is retained.
This Saishi is tsuma, ko, wife and children. The family sense is separate from the preceding homonymous ritual term.
Saishin is serving again, explained by futatabi susumu. The Portuguese begins the specific table-service sense of giving additional rice.

runs.text: ou Xiru que ſe dà duas, ou tres vezes na meſa,

lines.note: Rice or shiru is served two or three times at the table. Xiru, soup, is a Japanese food term embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
Saishin wo motte maire is an instruction to bring an additional serving. The Portuguese imperative Traze arroz begins its translation, which continues below.

runs.text: pera prouer os Goquis a ſegunda, ou 3. vez.

lines.note: The rice is brought to refill the Goquis for a second or third time. Goquis is the inflected name of the bowls within the Portuguese sentence; the printed numeral 3 is preserved.

runs.text: Vaſo, em que trazem eſte ar-

lines.note: Saishinbachi is the vessel used to bring this additional rice. Ar- begins arroz across the physical line division.
Roz completes ar-roz, specified as cooked rice brought to the table. The grave in à is retained from the print.
Saishiki is coloring or painting, explained by irodoru. The Portuguese gives painting in colors and continues with the manuscript-coloring sense below.
Illuminar completes the coloring gloss. Saishiki wo suru is the corresponding noun-plus-suru example and remains on this physical row.
The verbal entry Saixiqi gives its principal forms and again means illuminating or painting. The printed past form is preserved rather than remodeled into a modern conjugation.
Rias completes va-rias, specifying several colors. This is the continuation of the coloring verb rather than a separate sense of the next headword.
Saishoo denotes a particular office or dignity, with tsukasadoru katachi as its Japanese explanation. The Portuguese noun dignidade is divided across the line boundary.
Dade completes digni-dade, a rank or office. The brief row belongs to Saixǒ and is not omitted as empty-looking material.

Saisho is hajime, the beginning. The scan restores the missing i in Fajime and c in Principio. Saishoni starts an example that continues at the top of f433; the bottom catchword is recorded separately as furniture.
The damaged catchword reads yǔta and anticipates the first body word on bnf-f0433; the u bears a caron.
